newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan economic growth brightens recovery prospects.
newsitem.headline: Japan economic growth brightens recovery prospects.

text.p: Japan's economy posted solid growth in the final quarter of last year, brightening prospects for a sustainable recovery which can overcome temporary setbacks from a tax rise in April, economists said on Thursday.

The figure for the fiscal year starting on April 1 will probably be a little higher than the 2.5 percent government projection, said Takashi Kiuchi, chief economist at the Long-Term Credit Bank of Japan.
"All these indicate, the statistics are confirming, that the recovery is continuing a bit more strongly than before. I think this is a very good prelude for 1997 fiscal year," he said.

The nation's gross domestic product (GDP) -- the total output of goods and services minus net income from overseas production -- rose a real 1.0 percent in the October-December period from the previous quarter, or an annualised 3.9 percent.
This compared with a revised quarter-on-quarter GDP rise of 0.3 percent for the July-September quarter.

In calendar 1996, the nation's GDP -- a closely watched pointer to the health of the economy -- rose a real 3.6 percent from the previous year, after a revised figure of 1.4 percent growth in 1995, the Economic Planning Agency (EPA) said.
The annual growth rate rose over three percent for the first time in five years, the EPA said.

EPA Vice Minister Shimpei Nukaya told reporters that the growth in October-December period was led by private demand, which economists said was reflected in strong growth in capital spending, housing investments and private consumption.
The contribution to GDP from external demand -- net exports of goods and services -- stood at plus 0.4 percent while the contribution from domestic demand stood at plus 0.6 percent.

"These numbers show that the economy probably has a little more momentum than most people thought up until now. Companies are investing more, and they aren't completely irrational," said Kenneth Courtis, chief economist at Deutsche Bank Group.

Nukaya, who echoed economists' views on upbeat economic prospects, said that firm corporate capital spending and better employment conditions would put the economy back on a recovery track despite a fall in consumption from April.
"A slowing down (of economic growth) is likely but it will be temporary and the economy will return to steadier growth in the latter half of the year," he said.
Others were more pessimistic, saying it would be difficult to achieve the target GDP growth of 1.9 percent in 1997/98.

"There are already uncertainties looming on the horizon. Public-sector demand has already fallen and we are expecting fiscal tightening in the coming months. The effects from the extra budget (for 1996/97) are seen as temporary. I'd say that growth has peaked out (in October-December) for the time being," said Tomoko Fujii at Salomon Brothers Asia Ltd.

Japan's government is tightening purse strings in an effort to get its big budget deficit under control, and will raise the sales tax to five percent from three percent on April 1, end special income tax cuts and raise social security charges.
External demand is expected to offset the dampening effect of slower domestic demand on the economy in the coming months, especially in the April-June period, economists said.

"Growth in the April to June period will be dependent on external demand. If the United States takes note of that, we may see some response from them," said Yasuhiko Ushikubo, an economist at the Industrial Bank of Japan.
U.S. officials have raised concerns over Japan's growing trade surplus on the back of the weaker yen, and have warned Tokyo against trying to export its way out of domestic economic trouble.
But economists said Japan does not need additional fiscal steps to support its economy now, although it would need continued support from an easy monetary policy.

"I expect the Bank of Japan to keep the current easy credit stance throughout the next fiscal year. Rather than taking steps in advance, the BOJ would take time to confirm the recovery before making any moves," Fujii said.
